cases.title: Apollo 13 - Service Module oxygen tank 2 failure
cases.failure_mode: Wiring insulation fire and overpressure in a cryogenic oxygen tank
cases.sources: Report of the Apollo 13 Review Board (1970)
cases.failure_mode_description: Damaged electrical wiring insulation inside cryogenic oxygen tank 2 of the Service Module ignited when the tank fans were energised. Combustion raised tank pressure until the tank failed, removing the Service Module's oxygen supply and fuel-cell power and blowing off an external panel. The crew used the Lunar Module as a lifeboat, the landing was abandoned, and they returned safely.
cases.causal_chain: The tank had earlier been dropped about two inches during handling at the manufacturer's plant, which probably loosened its internal fill tube. During the countdown demonstration test before launch the tank could not be emptied normally, so its internal heaters were left on for hours to boil off the oxygen. The heaters' thermostatic protection switches were rated for the spacecraft's 28 V DC supply but not for the 65 V DC ground supply then in use; the switches welded closed, and temperatures in the heater tube may have reached about 1,000 deg F, severely damaging the Teflon insulation on the fan and heater wiring. The damage went unrecognised. At about 55 hours 54 minutes after launch, the crew performed a routine cryogenic stir, switching on the tank fans. Damaged wiring short-circuited and ignited the insulation. Combustion inside the tank raised its pressure and temperature over tens of seconds until the tank failed. The failure also caused oxygen tank 1 to leak, and fuel cells 1 and 3 lost their reactant supply.
telemetry_signatures: Hours before the event, the tank 2 quantity measurement failed off-scale high, an instrumentation anomaly inside the same tank.
Electrical current transients on the fan circuits shortly after the fans were switched on, indicating short circuits.
A rise in tank 2 pressure and temperature over roughly a minute and a half, then pressure falling abruptly to zero.
A telemetry dropout of about two seconds, with spacecraft attitude disturbances and a crew report of a bang.
Main bus B undervoltage, followed by fuel cell 1 and 3 failures and a slow, continuing decay of oxygen tank 1 pressure.
cases.root_cause: The Review Board concluded that the failure began with an electrical short and insulation fire inside oxygen tank 2. This was enabled by heater thermostatic switches incompatible with the 65 V ground supply, which let the heaters overheat and damage the insulation during pre-launch detanking. Contributing factors included the earlier drop, the unusual detanking procedure, combustible materials inside a high-pressure oxygen tank, and inadequate review of switch specifications when the ground supply voltage changed.
lessons_learned: An electrical event can initiate a pressure-vessel failure: look for current or voltage transients immediately before a pressure excursion.
Bus undervoltage and fuel-cell failures can be consequences of a reactant loss rather than the initiating cause.
An earlier instrumentation failure inside the same component is a warning sign, not just a sensor nuisance.
Correlate commanded actions (fan on, valve open) with anomaly onset.
Ground-test history, such as abnormal detanking, belongs in the hypothesis set.

cases.title: Space Shuttle Challenger STS-51-L - solid rocket booster field joint seal failure
cases.failure_mode: Solid rocket motor field joint O-ring seal failure and hot gas leak
cases.sources: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission, 1986)
cases.failure_mode_description: Hot combustion gas escaped past the O-ring seals of the aft field joint of the right solid rocket booster (SRB). The resulting plume impinged on the external tank and on the strut attaching the booster to the tank, leading to a hydrogen tank leak, failure of the aft attachment and structural breakup of the vehicle about 73 seconds after launch. All seven crew members were lost.
cases.causal_chain: The launch morning was unusually cold, with an ambient temperature of about 36 deg F, roughly 15 deg F colder than any previous launch. Cold reduced the resilience of the rubber O-rings, so they could not follow the opening of the joint gap ('joint rotation') when the motor pressurised at ignition. Puffs of black smoke seen in imagery near the right booster's aft field joint within the first second showed early blow-by. Combustion products appear to have temporarily sealed the gap. At around 37 seconds the vehicle encountered strong wind shear, and the resulting loads likely disturbed that temporary seal. A flame plume became visible at about 59 seconds and grew rapidly. It impinged on the external tank and the booster's aft attach strut. By about 64-66 seconds the external tank's liquid hydrogen tank was leaking. At about 72 seconds the aft attachment between the right booster and the external tank failed, the booster rotated, the hydrogen tank's aft dome failed, and at about 73 seconds the vehicle broke up under aerodynamic loads.
telemetry_signatures: No telemetry anomaly at ignition: the first physical cue (smoke at the joint) appeared only in imagery, about a minute before the first data anomaly.
Near 60 seconds, the right booster's chamber pressure began falling below the left booster's: an asymmetry between nominally identical units.
Increased steering activity of the booster nozzles and main engines counteracting the side force from the leak and wind loads.
Around 64-66 seconds, external tank liquid hydrogen ullage pressure dropped, indicating a leak.
In the final seconds, abrupt lateral accelerations and main engine propellant inlet pressure changes, followed by loss of data at about 73 seconds.
cases.root_cause: The Commission found the cause to be the failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right solid rocket motor. The joint design was unacceptably sensitive to temperature, dimensional tolerances, reuse, processing and joint loads. Contributing factors included decision-making that accepted repeated prior evidence of O-ring erosion and blow-by as normal, and engineering concerns about cold-temperature performance that were not effectively communicated to the launch decision.
lessons_learned: The initiating event can precede the first telemetry anomaly by a long time; include environmental conditions such as temperature in the hypothesis set.
Compare redundant or symmetric units (left vs. right booster) for divergence.
A pressure decay in an adjacent tank after a propulsion asymmetry suggests external damage spreading between subsystems.
Prior in-family anomalies (erosion, blow-by) should be trended, not normalised.

cases.title: Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107 - thermal protection breach from launch foam strike
cases.failure_mode: Wing leading edge thermal protection breach and re-entry burn-through
cases.sources: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I (2003)
cases.failure_mode_description: A breach in the reinforced carbon-carbon (RCC) thermal protection on the left wing leading edge let superheated air into the wing structure during re-entry. The hot gas progressively destroyed wiring and aluminium structure inside the wing, increasing drag on the left side until the flight control system could no longer hold attitude, and the orbiter broke up. All seven crew members were lost.
cases.causal_chain: About 82 seconds after launch, a piece of insulating foam of about 1.7 lb broke off the external tank's left bipod ramp. It struck the left wing leading edge near RCC panel 8 at a relative speed of roughly 545 mph, creating a breach. The strike was seen in launch imagery and analysed during the mission, but the damage was judged not to be a safety-of-flight issue, and no on-orbit imagery of the wing was obtained. On 1 February the orbiter began re-entry. Shortly after entry interface, plasma flowing through the breach heated the wing interior. Sensors behind the leading edge and in the left wheel well began showing unusual readings, then failed as their wiring burned through. Ground observers saw debris being shed. The growing damage increased left-wing drag, and the flight control system responded with increasing aileron trim and yaw-jet firings. Contact was lost shortly before 9:00 a.m. EST, and the orbiter broke up over Texas about 16 minutes before its scheduled landing.
telemetry_signatures: Early in re-entry, unusual strain and temperature rises on sensors inside the left wing (leading edge spar, wheel well, hydraulic lines) while right-wing sensors stayed nominal.
A spatial sequence of left-wing sensors failing off-scale low as their wiring burned through; off-scale low here meant destroyed wiring, not real cold.
Growing aileron trim and yaw reaction-control jet activity to counteract rising left-side drag.
Loss of left main landing gear tire pressure and wheel temperature indications shortly before loss of signal.
cases.root_cause: The Board found the physical cause to be a breach in the left wing leading edge thermal protection, initiated by the foam strike at launch. Organisational causes were given equal weight: foam shedding had occurred on earlier flights and had come to be treated as an accepted, maintenance-level risk rather than a safety issue; schedule pressure; and a safety culture in which engineering concerns and requests for imagery did not reach effective decision-making.
lessons_learned: A launch-phase event can cause a failure much later in the mission; carry known debris or impact events forward as hypotheses.
Sensors dropping off-scale in a spatial pattern indicate physical damage propagating, not independent sensor faults.
Left/right asymmetry between symmetric sensors is a strong localisation clue.
Rising control effort (trim, jet firings) can reveal an aerodynamic asymmetry before any structural measurement does.
Recurring 'in-family' anomalies should be treated as unresolved risks.

cases.title: Falcon 9 CRS-7 - second-stage LOX tank overpressure from a failed helium bottle strut
cases.failure_mode: COPV support strut failure causing helium release and LOX tank overpressure
cases.sources: SpaceX CRS-7 investigation update (July 2015); NASA Independent Review Team summary (2018)
cases.failure_mode_description: The second-stage liquid oxygen (LOX) tank overpressurised and burst about 139 seconds into flight, while the first stage was still firing, after a high-pressure helium bottle mounted inside the tank broke loose. The vehicle broke up and the Dragon cargo spacecraft bound for the International Space Station was lost.
cases.causal_chain: Helium pressurant for the second stage is stored in composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs) mounted inside the LOX tank with steel struts. Under the high axial acceleration of late first-stage flight (around 3.2 g), the buoyant helium bottle pulls hard on its struts. SpaceX's investigation found that one strut most likely failed at roughly 2,000 lbf, far below its 10,000 lbf rating. The bottle broke free, its plumbing failed, and high-pressure helium flooded the LOX tank faster than the relief system could vent it. The tank overpressurised and burst. From the first sign of trouble to loss of telemetry was under one second. The Dragon capsule survived the breakup and continued transmitting for some time, but its software at the time did not include a contingency mode to deploy its parachutes, so it was lost on impact with the ocean. NASA's Independent Review Team agreed that the strut failure was a credible cause, and also attributed the failure to a design error: the use of an industrial-grade cast part in a critical load path without adequate screening, testing or margin.
telemetry_signatures: A sudden pressure drop in the second-stage helium pressurisation system.
At the same moment, a rapid rise in second-stage LOX tank ullage pressure: opposite-sign changes in a pressurant source and the tank it feeds.
Timing during powered flight near peak axial acceleration, not at a planned transient such as staging or throttling.
An extremely short timeline (well under one second) from first anomaly to loss of signal.
cases.root_cause: SpaceX identified the most probable cause as structural failure of a COPV support strut under flight loads, releasing helium into the LOX tank. The NASA review team considered the strut a credible cause but noted that other contributing failure paths could not be fully excluded, and emphasised the design and part-qualification decisions. Corrective actions included replacing the struts and qualifying parts individually.
lessons_learned: Simultaneous opposite-sign pressure changes in connected volumes indicate an internal leak path between them.
Structural failures of internal hardware tend to occur at peak load; check the acceleration profile at the anomaly time.
When the timeline to loss of signal is sub-second, high-rate data near the anomaly is critical; low-rate telemetry may show only the end state.
Contingency modes for payload recovery should be considered for failures outside the planned sequence.

cases.title: Falcon 9 AMOS-6 - pad anomaly during propellant loading from a second-stage COPV failure
cases.failure_mode: Helium COPV failure inside the second-stage LOX tank during loading
cases.sources: SpaceX AMOS-6 anomaly updates (September 2016 and January 2017); investigation with FAA, NASA and U.S. Air Force participation
cases.failure_mode_description: During propellant loading at Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral, in preparation for a pre-launch static fire test, the Falcon 9 vehicle was destroyed by a fast-developing fire and explosion that started in the second stage. The AMOS-6 communications satellite, already mounted on the vehicle, was lost and the pad was heavily damaged. No one was injured. No engines were running at the time.
cases.causal_chain: The second stage stores helium in composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs) submerged in the liquid oxygen (LOX) tank. Falcon 9 used densified, sub-cooled LOX and very cold helium, loaded on a tight timeline. SpaceX reported that early data indicated a large breach in the second stage's cryogenic helium system, and that the time from the first sign of anomaly to loss of data was about 93 milliseconds. The investigation concluded that one of the three COPVs inside the second-stage LOX tank failed. Its most likely explanation was that liquid or solid oxygen accumulated in voids or buckles between the COPV's aluminium liner and its carbon overwrap. Under the loading conditions, friction or fiber breakage in this oxygen-rich region could ignite the carbon composite, leading to rupture of the COPV and of the LOX tank. Test campaigns reproduced failures of this kind under similar conditions. The loading temperature and pressure of the helium were identified as factors that made the condition possible.
telemetry_signatures: A static vehicle on the pad, no engine operation, during the propellant and helium loading phase.
A sudden drop in second-stage helium system pressure, indicating a large breach.
Near-simultaneous disturbances in second-stage LOX tank pressure and temperature as helium and combustion products entered the tank.
Loss of data roughly 93 milliseconds after the first anomalous indication: an event far faster than any operator response.
cases.root_cause: SpaceX and the participating agencies concluded that the most likely cause was failure of a helium COPV inside the second-stage LOX tank, caused by oxygen accumulating between the liner and overwrap in a buckle or void and then igniting. SpaceX's corrective actions in the short term changed the COPV configuration and loading procedures to use warmer helium and loading conditions closer to those previously flown successfully, and in the longer term redesigned the COPVs to prevent liner buckling.
lessons_learned: Ground operations such as propellant loading are hazardous phases; anomaly detection must cover them, not just flight.
Sub-second events require high-rate, time-synchronised data; slow telemetry may only capture the end state.
Changes in loading temperature, pressure or timeline are prime suspects when a new failure appears.
Composite pressure vessels submerged in liquid oxygen have failure modes involving oxygen compatibility, not just pressure loads.

cases.title: Starship Integrated Flight Test 1 - booster engine losses, loss of control and flight termination
cases.failure_mode: Aft-section propellant leak and fire causing engine losses and loss of vehicle control
cases.sources: SpaceX Starship Flight Test summary and mishap investigation update (2023); FAA statements (2023)
cases.failure_mode_description: On the first integrated flight of Starship and Super Heavy from Starbase, Texas, several booster Raptor engines were lost during ascent, the vehicle lost attitude control, the planned stage separation did not occur, and the autonomous flight termination system was activated. The vehicle broke up over the Gulf of Mexico about four minutes after liftoff. The launch also severely damaged the launch pad, which had no flame deflector or water deluge system.
cases.causal_chain: Several Raptor engines were not running or shut down early in the ascent, and more were lost as the flight continued. SpaceX's investigation, overseen by the FAA, identified the most likely root cause for the loss of control as propellant leaks in the aft section of the Super Heavy booster. The leaks led to fires in the engine bay that severed connections with the primary flight computer. That caused loss of communication with most booster engines and, ultimately, loss of control of the vehicle. The vehicle tumbled, and stage separation was not achieved. The flight termination system was triggered, but the vehicle took considerably longer than expected to break up after activation, which SpaceX also addressed. Debris from the damaged pad was widely discussed as a possible contributor to early engine problems, but SpaceX's public summary attributed the loss of control to the aft-section leak and fire; the exact contribution of pad debris is less certain.
telemetry_signatures: Engine-out indications on several booster Raptors from liftoff through early ascent, with the count growing over time.
Indications consistent with fire in the booster aft section (SpaceX reported fires there) before engine communication was lost.
Loss of communication between the flight computer and many engines at once: a shared-cause signature (wiring or avionics damage) rather than independent engine faults.
Attitude and trajectory departures, then tumbling, without the planned stage separation event.
Flight termination activation followed by a delay of tens of seconds before breakup and loss of signal.
cases.root_cause: SpaceX identified the most likely root cause as propellant leaks in the booster aft section that caused fires, severing connections to the primary flight computer and leading to loss of engine communication and vehicle control. The FAA closed the mishap investigation with a list of required corrective actions, including vehicle hardware redesigns to prevent leaks and fires, flight termination system changes, and launch pad improvements such as a water-cooled steel flame deflector.
lessons_learned: Many engines dropping out together points to a shared cause (fire, power, data bus) rather than many independent engine failures.
Distinguish an engine shutdown commanded by its controller from an engine that simply stopped reporting.
Aft-bay temperature trends are an early warning of leaks and fires before engines are affected.
Ground infrastructure damage can create debris and environmental hazards that must be considered in the causal chain.

cases.title: Starship Integrated Flight Test 2 - Super Heavy booster loss during boostback
cases.failure_mode: LOX filter blockage causing low turbopump inlet pressure and energetic engine failure
cases.sources: SpaceX Starship Flight Test 2 summary (2024); FAA statements (2024)
cases.failure_mode_description: Loss of oxidizer turbopump inlet pressure on multiple Raptor engines during the booster's boostback burn, followed by an energetic engine failure and loss of the booster. The upper stage (Ship) was lost later in the flight from a separate cause, a leak and fire in its aft section.
cases.causal_chain: All 33 booster engines operated through ascent, and the vehicle completed the first successful hot-stage separation. Shortly after the booster began its boostback burn, several Raptor engines started shutting down, and one engine then failed energetically; the booster was lost roughly three and a half minutes into flight. SpaceX identified the most likely root cause as a filter blockage where liquid oxygen (LOX) is supplied to the engines. The blockage reduced LOX inlet pressure at the engines' oxidizer turbopumps. Insufficient pump inlet pressure is the classic precondition for cavitation, which degrades pump performance and can damage turbomachinery. The degraded engines shut down, and one failed in a way that destroyed the vehicle. Separately, the Ship continued its ascent burn. Near the end of the burn, liquid oxygen was vented as planned, and SpaceX reported that a leak in the aft section that developed when LOX was vented led to a combustion event and fires. These caused a loss of communication between the ship's flight computers, a commanded shutdown of all six engines before burn completion, and activation of the autonomous flight safety system about eight minutes into flight.
telemetry_signatures: Falling oxidizer pump inlet pressure on several engines at the same time: a shared-feed symptom (tank, filter, ducting), not a single-engine fault.
Engine shutdowns clustered in time during a manoeuvre that disturbs propellant settling (reorientation and boostback).
Turbopump speed and vibration excursions on the affected engines.
A rapid pressure and vibration transient immediately before booster loss of signal.
On the Ship, aft-section temperature rises after the LOX vent, followed by loss of flight-computer communication and engine shutdown.
cases.root_cause: Booster: blockage of the LOX supply filtration, causing low oxidizer turbopump inlet pressure and an engine failure. Reported corrective actions included hardware changes inside booster oxidizer tanks to improve propellant filtration and refined operations. Ship: an aft-section leak and fire associated with the LOX vent; corrective actions included hardware changes to prevent leaks and improve fire protection.
lessons_learned: When inlet pressure falls first and turbopump vibration follows within seconds, treat the feed system as the initiating cause and turbopump distress as a consequence (possible cavitation).
Correlated faults across engines sharing a feed point to common hardware upstream.
Propellant management events (vents, slosh) are plausible triggers for leaks and feed problems.
Two stages can fail from unrelated causes on the same flight; analyse each stage's timeline separately.

cases.title: Starship Integrated Flight Test 3 - booster landing burn failure and ship loss during re-entry
cases.failure_mode: Booster engine shutdowns during return burns; ship roll control loss before re-entry
cases.sources: SpaceX Starship Flight 3 summary (2024); FAA statements (2024)
cases.failure_mode_description: The third integrated flight achieved a full ascent and hot-stage separation, and the Ship reached its planned coast trajectory for the first time. Both stages were then lost: the Super Heavy booster had engine shutdowns during its return burns and was lost before splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico, and the Ship was lost during re-entry after it was unable to control its roll attitude.
cases.causal_chain: After hot staging, the booster performed its boostback burn, during which some engines shut down early. During the landing burn attempt, the booster did not achieve the planned engine operation and was lost a few hundred metres above the water. SpaceX's post-flight summary attributed the booster engine problems most likely to blockage in the oxidizer supply to the engines, a theme similar to Flight 2; the exact mechanism is less certain in public sources. The Ship completed its ascent burn and coasted, performing a payload door test and an in-flight propellant transfer demonstration. During the coast it developed roll rates higher than expected, and the planned in-space Raptor relight was skipped. SpaceX attributed the roll control problem most likely to clogging of valves used for roll control. Without proper attitude control, the Ship entered the atmosphere in an off-nominal orientation, experienced higher-than-planned heating, and signal was lost roughly 49 minutes into flight, well before the planned splashdown in the Indian Ocean. The FAA oversaw the SpaceX-led mishap investigation and accepted its findings.
telemetry_signatures: Booster: engine shutdowns during the boostback burn, followed by an incomplete or failed landing burn and loss of signal at low altitude.
Booster: oxidizer inlet pressure anomalies on multiple engines, a shared-feed signature (less certain detail in public data).
Ship: growing roll rate during coast despite control commands, with attitude-control valve or thruster performance below expectation.
Ship: cancellation of a planned engine relight due to unsuitable attitude conditions.
Ship: off-nominal attitude during re-entry, rising heating indications and loss of signal well before planned splashdown.
cases.root_cause: SpaceX identified clogging of roll control valves as the most likely cause of the Ship's attitude control loss, leading to an uncontrolled re-entry; reported corrective actions included adding roll control thrusters and improving resilience to clogging. For the booster, SpaceX attributed the engine shutdowns most likely to oxidizer supply blockage and reported hardware improvements to filtration; this detail is less certain than the Ship finding.
lessons_learned: A flight can fail in independent ways on each stage; build separate timelines before searching for common causes.
A control rate that grows while commands saturate indicates actuator or valve degradation, not a guidance fault.
Attitude control problems in coast directly raise re-entry thermal risk; flag them as precursors.
Recurring feed-system blockages across flights suggest a systemic contamination or design issue.

cases.title: Antares Orb-3 - first-stage engine turbopump failure shortly after liftoff
cases.failure_mode: LOX turbopump failure in an AJ26 first-stage engine
cases.vehicle: Orbital Sciences Antares 130 with Cygnus (Orb-3 / CRS mission)
cases.sources: Orbital Sciences Accident Investigation Board findings (2015); NASA Independent Review Team report on the Orb-3 accident (2015)
cases.failure_mode_description: Seconds after liftoff from Wallops Island, Virginia, one of the two AJ26 engines on the Antares first stage failed catastrophically. The vehicle lost thrust and fell back towards the launch pad, the flight termination system was activated, and the rocket and its Cygnus cargo spacecraft bound for the International Space Station were destroyed. The launch pad was significantly damaged. No one was injured.
cases.causal_chain: The Antares first stage was powered by two AJ26 engines, which were modified NK-33 engines originally built in the Soviet Union decades earlier and refurbished and tested in the United States. Liftoff appeared normal. A few seconds into flight, a failure occurred in the liquid oxygen (LOX) turbopump of one engine, causing an explosion in the engine compartment and loss of thrust. The vehicle began to descend, and the range safety flight termination system was activated, with the vehicle impacting near the pad. The investigations agreed that the failure originated in the LOX turbopump, but differed on the underlying cause. Orbital's investigation concluded the most likely cause was a design deficiency in the turbopump's hydrostatic bearing, leading to bearing failure and rubbing that ignited the pump. NASA's Independent Review Team agreed that the turbopump was the source but could not identify a single root cause; it listed credible causes including inadequate design robustness of the bearing, foreign object debris in the pump, and manufacturing defects, and noted that foreign object debris could not be ruled out. An AJ26 engine had also failed during ground testing earlier in 2014.
telemetry_signatures: Nominal ignition and liftoff, with the anomaly appearing seconds into flight rather than at a transient.
Turbopump speed and vibration anomalies on one engine, with the second engine nominal: a single-engine fault signature.
Abrupt loss of thrust and chamber pressure on the affected engine, with engine compartment temperature and pressure indications of fire or explosion.
Vehicle acceleration turning negative and attitude disturbances, followed by flight termination and loss of signal.
cases.root_cause: The failure originated in the LOX turbopump of one AJ26 engine. Orbital attributed it most likely to a hydrostatic bearing design deficiency; NASA's review team identified several credible causes, including bearing design, foreign object debris and manufacturing defects, without a single definitive root cause. Orbital subsequently replaced the AJ26 with RD-181 engines.
lessons_learned: Asymmetry between two engines on one stage localises the fault quickly.
Turbopump vibration and speed trends are leading indicators of bearing distress; trend them against acceptance-test data.
Aging or refurbished hardware with a prior test-stand failure history deserves elevated scrutiny.
When investigations disagree, keep all credible causes in the hypothesis set.

cases.title: Delta II GPS IIR-1 - solid rocket motor case rupture shortly after liftoff
cases.failure_mode: Composite solid rocket motor case rupture from pre-flight damage
cases.vehicle: Delta II 7925 (McDonnell Douglas, now Boeing) with GPS IIR-1 satellite
cases.sources: U.S. Air Force and launch provider accident investigation findings (1997)
cases.failure_mode_description: About 13 seconds after liftoff from Cape Canaveral, one of the nine graphite-epoxy strap-on solid rocket motors (GEM) of the Delta II ruptured. The rupture destroyed the vehicle and its payload, the first Block IIR GPS satellite. Burning propellant and debris fell over the launch complex area, damaging facilities and parked vehicles. No one was injured.
cases.causal_chain: The Delta II 7925 configuration used nine Graphite Epoxy Motors around the first stage, six ignited at liftoff and three in the air. Investigators concluded that the composite case of one of the ground-lit motors had a crack or split that let hot gas escape shortly after ignition. The case breached about 13 seconds into flight, and the motor broke apart. The resulting failure tore into the first stage and the adjacent motors, and the vehicle was destroyed; destruct systems then terminated the remaining stages. The investigation concluded that the most probable cause was damage to the motor case that occurred before flight, likely during handling or transport, and was not detected by inspection. Damage to a filament-wound composite case can be internal and invisible from the outside, so routine visual inspection could not reliably detect it. Delta II flights resumed later in 1997 after the investigation, and the GPS IIR series went on to fly successfully on subsequent launches.
telemetry_signatures: Nominal ignition and early ascent, with the anomaly occurring within seconds of liftoff during peak solid motor pressure.
An abrupt drop in chamber pressure on one strap-on motor relative to its nominally identical neighbours.
Sudden lateral and roll disturbances and steering activity from the asymmetric thrust and structural damage.
Breakup and flight termination within a fraction of a second to a few seconds, followed by loss of signal.
cases.root_cause: The most probable cause was a split in the composite case of one GEM solid rocket motor, resulting from pre-flight handling or transport damage that went undetected. Corrective actions reported publicly included improved handling procedures and inspection of composite motor cases before flight.
lessons_learned: Composite structures can conceal damage; handling history belongs in root-cause analysis.
Compare identical strap-on motors for pressure divergence; one diverging unit localises the failure.
An anomaly in the first seconds of flight, at peak pressure, points towards a pre-existing defect rather than a flight-induced one.
Very short timelines mean the anomaly onset in high-rate data is the most valuable evidence.
